item.title: Earth from Space: Namibia’s biggest salt pan
item.summary: Image: This image from Copernicus Sentinel-2, acquired on 5 April 2026, shows the Etosha National Park in northern Namibia.
item.page_text:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
This image from Copernicus Sentinel-2 , acquired on 5 April 2026, shows the Etosha National Park in northern Namibia.
Zoom in to explore this image at its full resolution.
The area is a game reserve featuring a large salt flat – the Etosha Pan – as well as numerous smaller salt pans, with vegetation shown in red in this false-colour image.
The Etosha Pan, which spans roughly 130 km from east to west and covers 4760 sq km, appears bright white to human eyes. The colours in this image, however, range from the white expanses of salt to light blue where water contains cloudy sediment, and dark blue where the water is clearer.
The image was acquired at the beginning of the dry season, when average daily temperatures typically range from 14°C to 30°C. Water is also still present in the smaller salt pans that dot the landscape northwest of the Etosha Pan, the biggest of which is the Natukanaoka Pan. The water in these small ‘lakes’ appears in shades of green and blue.
The Ekuma river, near the centre of the image, is seen flowing from Lake Oponono at an elevation of about 1200 m above sea level, southwards to the salt flat at 1030 m. Lake Oponono is able to hold water from one wet season to the next and is a habitat for flamingos and cattle.
The vegetation surrounding the Etosha Pan – shown in striking red by Sentinel-2’s near-infrared channel – consists mainly of grassland, savannas and mopane woodland. Mopane trees are the dominant type of vegetation across the eastern and central areas of the national park, showing up as dark, vibrant red in this image. They provide a habitat for elephants, giraffe and leopards. The savannahs, in the west and southern areas of the park, are home to wildebeest, lions and springbok.
Patches of red are also visible on the Etosha Pan, suggesting vegetation is present. While few plants thrive in the salty clay terrain, some types of blue-green algae and salt-tolerant grasses have adapted to the harsh environment.
Sentinel-2 carries a multispectral imager, which detects light in 13 spectral bands – in contrast to the human eye, which can see only three spectral bands (red, blue and green). This allows the mission to capture near-infrared and short-wave infrared light, creating false-colour images that highlight specific features on the landscape. Since healthy plants reflect more near-infrared light, the areas with vibrant red correlate to areas where vegetation is dense.

Near-infrared renders vegetation red, with mopane woodland in the east and centre of the park at its darkest. item.title: Mapping the Cosmos
item.summary: Want to explore the night sky? Two new interactive maps offer very different ways to do it. Skyviewer lets you explore the vast astronomical survey being created by the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory , while Stargazing for Beginners helps you work out what you can actually see in the sky above you. Skyviewer is an interactive window onto Rubin Observatory's survey of the cosmos. Located in Chile, Rubin will repeatedly scan the sky for the next ten years, creating an enormous time-lapse record of the changing universe. You can use Skyviewer to explore the results from these scans, navigating around Rubin's imagery to discover stars, galaxies and other celestial objects. The experience also includes Skysynth , which turns this visual exploration into a sonified journey through the cosmos. If Skyviewer is about exploring the universe, Stargazing for Beginners is about exploring the sky above your head. The interactive sky map uses your location and the current time to show what is visible, with a mobile orientation mode that lets you point your phone at the sky to identify objects. You can speed up time to watch the sky change over hours or days, filter objects by type and limiting mag

item.title: Sentinel-3C returns its first views of Earth
item.summary: Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments – a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on the road to monitoring the health of Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.
item.page_text:
Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments – a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on the road to monitoring the health of Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.
This first set of images includes stunning views of Italy, the Arctic and the Caribbean from the satellite’s ocean and land colour instrument, as well as measurements of the height of the Greenland ice sheet and sea surface from its synthetic aperture radar altimeter.
Sentinel-3C is the third satellite in the Sentinel-3 series and will continue the mission’s long-term task of delivering environmental data that are essential for a wide range of applications.
As the workhorse mission for Copernicus, the Sentinel-3 satellites carry the same suite of instruments to measure systematically Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.
Over oceans, Sentinel-3 measures the temperature, colour and height of the sea surface as well as the thickness of sea ice to support, for example, the monitoring of marine pollution and marine heatwaves.
Over land, this innovative mission monitors drought and wildfires, maps the way land is used, checks vegetation health, and measures the height of rivers, lakes, and polar ice sheets as shown in the animation of Greenland below.
Sentinel-3's observations are also particularly valuable for providing near-realtime parameters for weather forecasting and for monitoring long-term changes associated with climate change.
The European Space Agency is still in the process of commissioning Sentinel-3C for service, an important and intricate task that will take another five months, but after only two weeks in orbit, the satellite’s initial images already showcase that it is on the road to excellence.
The first image, captured by the ocean and land colour instrument on 30 September, is a striking natural-colour view that reveals Italy in beautiful detail, stretching from southern Germany in the north to Sicily and the southern Mediterranean.
Just above the centre of the image, the broad, flat expanse of the Po Valley – Italy’s agricultural heartland – stands out in shades of brown and green. Just to the north, the snow-capped Alps form a dramatic contrast with the lowlands, their bright peaks clearly visible against the surrounding landscape. Across the rest of Italy, variations in green and brown reflect differences in vegetation, agriculture and other types of land cover.
To the east, the deep blue waters of the Adriatic Sea separate Italy from the Balkan Peninsula, which is partially visible in the image. Noticeable variations in sea colour can be seen along Italy’s eastern coastline, where lighter blue waters hug the shore. These brighter tones are likely caused by sediment carried into the sea by rivers and transported along the coast.
On Italy’s western side, the dark waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea surround the islands of Sardinia and Sicily, which are clearly visible, while Corsica is largely obscured by cloud. Together, the contrasting colours of the land, snow-covered mountains and surrounding seas provide a vivid view of Italy’s diverse landscape from space.
The second image, also captured by the ocean and land colour instrument on 30 September, features part of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, to the west of Greenland. Snow- and ice-covered islands dominate the scene, with rugged coastlines, deep fjords and exposed rock creating intricate patterns. At this time of the year sea ice is at a minimum but some fractured floes are visible on the dark open water.
The Arctic is warming much faster than the global average, causing rapid melting of ice on land and ice in the sea, which leads to further warming through feedback loops. Sentinel-3’s different instruments measure ice in different ways – all contributing to a better understanding of the vulnerable polar regions.
The third image captured on 29 September, also by the ocean and land colour instrument, is a spectacular view of part of the Caribbean, with Cuba to the south and the Bahamas towards the top of the image. Shallow waters around the islands appear in a beautiful turquoise set against the darker deeper waters of the open sea.
Low-lying islands and coastal regions around the world are at risk of sea-level rise. Sentinel-3’s synthetic aperture radar altimeter measures changes in the height of the sea surface to help monitor rising seas and contribute to action on climate change and mitigation strategies.
The map above shows measurements of sea-surface height across the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea from Sentinel-3C’s synthetic aperture radar altimeter, compared to the Copernicus Marine Service multimission sea-level anomaly. These new data demonstrate that the altimeter is performing well and comparable to current measurements. Once commissioned, the altimeter will contribute to monitoring changes in sea-surface height around the world, complementing long-term records from missions such as Copernicus Sentinel-6 and Jason.
High-precision satellite altimetry has enabled scientists to establish the rate of global sea-level rise, which has averaged 3.64 mm per year since 1999 , with the rate of rise accelerating.
The altimeter will also measure changes in the height of lakes, rivers, sea ice and land ice, also complementing the upcoming Copernicus CRISTAL mission.
The animation above shows measurements of the height of the Greenland Ice Sheet acquired by Sentinel-3C between 30 September and 4 October. The measurements also demonstrate that the altimeter is performing well, with all of the measurement tracks closely matching the reference digital elevation model.
Monitoring changes in the height of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets is essential for understanding the impacts of climate change and, importantly, for improving predictions of future sea-level rise. Ice loss from the sheets is a major con

why: Sentinel-3C first instrument returns, a concrete sensor milestone, though the post is more a status update than a visual story.

draft.what_it_shows: First images and measurements from Copernicus Sentinel-3C, about two weeks after launch. The lead visual is a natural-colour image from the satellite's ocean and land colour instrument, captured on 30 September. It shows Italy from southern Germany to Sicily: the Po Valley in brown and green, the snow-capped Alps, and lighter blue water along the Adriatic coast that ESA says is likely river sediment. Other first-light products are natural-colour views of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago (30 September) and Cuba and the Bahamas (29 September), a sea-surface height map from the synthetic aperture radar altimeter compared with the Copernicus Marine Service multimission sea-level anomaly, and Greenland Ice Sheet height tracks (30 September to 4 October) that closely match a reference digital elevation model.

The source does not give the launch date, only 'two weeks after it was launched'.

posts.linkedin:
The third Sentinel-3 satellite is in orbit and its first data look consistent with the rest of the constellation, which is the result that matters most for long-term records.

@esa has released the first images from Sentinel-3C's ocean and land colour instrument, including a natural-colour view of Italy captured on 30 September. The image shows the Po Valley, the Alps and lighter coastal water along the Adriatic that ESA attributes, with a 'likely', to river sediment. For data users, the more significant release is from the synthetic aperture radar altimeter. Its sea-surface height measurements were compared with the Copernicus Marine Service multimission sea-level anomaly, and its Greenland Ice Sheet tracks (30 September to 4 October) closely match a reference digital elevation model.

The practical implication is continuity. #Sentinel3 feeds sea surface temperature, ocean colour, sea ice, inland water height and vegetation monitoring, as well as near-realtime inputs for weather forecasting. Sentinel-3C's altimeter is meant to complement Sentinel-6, Jason and the upcoming CRISTAL mission. The caveats are clear, though. Commissioning will take another five months, and 'performing well' is not yet backed by published accuracy figures, so these products are not ready for operational use.
